takeaways: Every control tells assistive technology what it is (role), what it is called (name) and what state it is in (value and states).
When the state changes, such as expanded, checked or selected, assistive technology is told.
Developers build this. Designers decide the name, every state, and which standard component a design really is.
Native controls do this for free. A custom-drawn dropdown or toggle has to rebuild all of it.
failures: A clickable div that is not announced as a button
An icon-only button with no name
An accordion that never says if it is expanded
check: For each custom component, name the standard control it behaves like: button, link, checkbox, tab, switch.
List every state it can show, and check each one is drawn and named.
Give every icon-only control a name in the file.

quiz.question: Your design shows a “Filters” chip that opens a panel and shows a count when filters are on. What do you hand off?
options: The chip’s visual states only. Developers will work out the rest
Role: button. Name: “Filters”. States: expanded or collapsed, and the active count in the name
quiz.why: Role, name and state are design decisions. Without them, developers guess, and screen readers hear a generic or misleading control.

spec: Write the role of each custom component, using standard names like button, switch or tab.
Write the accessible name of every icon-only control.
List the states to expose, such as expanded, selected, checked, pressed or disabled.
review: What is this control, really? A link, a button, a tab?
What would a screen reader call it?
Which states here exist only visually?
tradeoff: Custom components give brand control but cost accessibility work in every one. Style native or well-tested library components where you can, and build custom only when the experience truly needs it.
system: Document each component’s role, name source and exposed states beside its visual spec, so every use inherits them.
pitch: If assistive technology cannot tell what a control is, the control does not exist for its users.
